question.text: The page gives 14,600 bytes as how much data fits in a TCP connection's initial congestion window — ten segments of 1,460 bytes each, on a standard 1,500-byte Ethernet MTU. Is 14,600 a fixed property of TCP itself?
options: No — it follows from a standard default (a 10-segment initial window) and a standard MTU; either one can differ on a real path or server
Yes — the TCP protocol specification fixes the initial congestion window at exactly 10 segments for every connection
No — TCP doesn't have an initial congestion window at all; this describes a legacy setting removed after Linux 2.6
Yes — 1,460 bytes per segment is a hard limit set by the IP packet header, not a configurable default
question.hint: Two numbers multiply to get 14,600: a segment count and a segment size. Are either of those numbers required by the protocol itself, or just what's typically configured?

explain.g: 14,600 is what you get from combining two common defaults, not a law of networking. A path with a smaller maximum packet size, or a server configured with a different starting window, gets a different number in the same slot of the same calculation. It's the standard case, not a universal constant.
explain.y: 10 segments × 1,460-byte payload (which itself comes from a 1,500-byte Ethernet MTU minus IP/TCP headers) = 14,600. The 10-segment initial congestion window is RFC 6928's recommendation, not a mandate baked into TCP's design; it's been the Linux default since kernel 2.6.39, but other stacks or manual tuning can set it differently, and a smaller-MTU path changes the other factor.
explain.r: RFC 6928 (IETF, April 2013); default in Linux since kernel 2.6.39 (May 2011). Networks with a smaller MTU — many VPNs, some mobile links — reduce the per-segment payload below 1,460, and servers running an older kernel or custom sysctl can carry a different initial cwnd. Both inputs to this number are configuration, not protocol invariants.
